newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan's Lee urges party to drop "ruler's attitude".
newsitem.headline: Taiwan's Lee urges party to drop "ruler's attitude".

text.p: Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui urged his ruling Nationalist Party to abandon its "ruler's attitude" and press ahead with internal reforms under fierce competition from rival parties.
"We must change our attitude. We can no longer adopt a ruler's attitude," Lee, who doubles as chairman of the Nationalists, said at an annual seminar on party affairs.
"We must continue reconstruction of the party organisation and raise the party's competitiveness...to ensure our party's status as the ruling party," he said.
The Nationalists have ruled Taiwan since the Republic of China government of "generalissimo" Chiang Kai-shek lost a civil war to Mao Zedong's communists and fled into exile on the island in 1949.
More than four decades of tough Nationalist authoritarianism have left many of Taiwan's 21 million people yearning for political and social liberalisation, even as their economy flourished.
The 2.6 million-member party's once-unshaken power started to weaken after Taiwan lifted martial law in 1987, allowing the establishment of the first legal opposition party.
The Nationalists suffered a sobering shock in the last general elections in December 1995, mustering only a razor-thin 51 percent majority in the 164-seat parliament.

Party reformers have pushed to replace old-school officials with younger, more service-minded officials to counter what has been a widespread public perception of the Nationalists as arrogant and unresponsive.

An increasing number of young and well-educated Taiwanese have defected to the fledgling New Party, formed in 1993 by a group of the Nationalist elite who accused the ruling party of failing to carry out internal reforms.

Taiwan's oldest opposition, the Democratic Progressive Party, has performed strongly against the Nationalists, taking the second-largest block of seats in parliament and winning many key mayoralties, including that of the capital, Taipei.
The Democratic Progressives lean toward Taiwan's independence rather than reunification with the Chinese mainland, which is a mainstay Nationalist policy.

More recently, the planned Taiwan Independence Party has begun wooing ardent supporters of a sovereign Republic of Taiwan away from the Democratic Progressive Party, which it says is not sufficiently committed to total independence from China.

"We cannot hesitate and we cannot wait," Lee said. "Only by marching forward bravely and struggling endlessly can we ensure the Chinese Nationalist Party's privilege in competition and create a new era for the party."
